extracted.intended_audience: scientists, lecturers, instrument makers, and readers of Nature (early 20th-century scientific community)
extracted.subtask_description: Specifications, observational criteria, and theoretical/experimental diagnostics for laboratory and lecture apparatus (projection lanterns, measurement rigs, condensers, microscopes, and choice of materials) and summaries of experimental diagnostic criteria from short research notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale resolution and magnification for expansion measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: The scale was divided into millimetres, each millimetre representing 1/1200-inch expansion, corresponding to a magnification of 48:1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design measurement scales with sufficient resolution and magnification to detect the small expansions under study (specifically here 1/1200-inch per mm at 48:1 magnification) so that thermal expansion of rods can be read accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain apparatus suitability by testing on standard materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The suitability and delicacy of the apparatus were ascertained by testing bars of wrought iron and steel; from the former a regular line was obtained, while the latter gave a curve showing a marked change of volume at the critical point (about 690°C), thus agreeing with Le Chatelier's results obtained by an entirely different method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate new measurement apparatus against well-characterized reference materials and known phenomena; concordance with established results (e.g., Le Chatelier) is evidence of correctness and sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility across material conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard-drawn copper bars gave a perfectly regular line, similar to that obtained with wrought iron; annealed copper also gave a straight line. Experiments on rods of brass of different composition, on gun-metal, and on phosphor bronze gave similar results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the apparatus produces consistent, reproducible measurements across different materials and treatments (e.g., hard-drawn vs annealed) to demonstrate robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mechanical/annealing changes from allotropic or chemical changes by volume/length behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: The change from the hard, elastic condition of worked copper and copper alloys to that of extremely soft metal is not accompanied by any alteration in length. On the other hand, allotropic changes in an element (e.g., pure iron at about 880°) or chemical constitutional changes (iron-carbon alloys at critical temperatures) are accompanied by marked alterations in volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measurements of length and volume changes to classify whether observed changes are mechanical/structural (internal rearrangement) or genuine allotropic/chemical transitions; different orders of change imply different interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize new cathode dark space by length and dependence on conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the new dark space, which under measurable conditions varies from 0.1 mm to 1.0 mm, is almost unaffected by the pressure of the gas, but varies roughly with the inverse square root of the current density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify the dark space by direct length measurement and report its functional dependence on control parameters (pressure, current density); these dependencies are diagnostic of the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use constant fall of potential across dark space as diagnostic per gas
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful observations show that the fall of potential across the new dark space is constant for the same gas under all observed conditions, and is in helium 30 volts, in hydrogen 15 volts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure potential drops across regions precisely; a gas-specific constant potential drop is a key diagnostic and can be used to infer the ionisation energy required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret dark space distance in terms of electron energy acquisition (theoretical diagnostic)
rubrics_metrics.description: An electron liberated from the surface of the cathode virtually at rest must fall freely through a definite potential in order to acquire the energy required to ionise a molecule; the new dark space may be regarded as the distance through which the electrons fall to attain sufficient energy to ionise the gas by collision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate measured spatial extents to potential differences and ionisation thresholds; use this physical picture to predict phenomena such as striations (successive maxima of ionisation at multiples of the basic potential).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine measured potentials with fundamental constants to estimate ionisation energy and electron velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining the potential differences obtained from the length of the new dark space with the accepted values of e and m for the electron, values of the energy required to ionise and the velocity of the ionising electron are obtained (numerical values reported for hydrogen and helium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured electrical potentials together with known electron charge and mass to calculate ionisation energies and electron velocities; present numerical estimates when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply isotropic-particle assembly theory to dispersion of double refraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a theory of the optical properties of a homogeneous assemblage of isotropic particles: if the medium behaves like a uniaxial crystal, the double refraction (difference between two principal indices) is proportional to a specified function of the mean index; the formula gives a law of dispersion of the double refraction provided the dispersion of the mean index is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model dispersion by considering both particle polarizability and spatial arrangement; validate theoretical formulas against experimental data (e.g., carbon disulphide under electric field, quartz over a wide range).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions connecting dispersion behaviour to crystal packing and cavity shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the crystal unit contains vibrating electrons; differences of packing of the crystal molecules are represented optically by variations in the ratios of the axes of the effective cavity (slightly ellipsoidal instead of spherical) and their directions relative to the polarisation axes of the unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing models of optical dispersion, include both microscopic electron behaviour and macroscopic packing effects (effective cavity geometry) as sufficient approximations to explain observed varieties of dispersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design features required in a science lantern for lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Lantern includes a hinged mirror placed at an angle of 45° in a short box to reflect the beam through a horizontal converging lens; an objective mounted on a pillar, with a prism silvered on the outside reflecting the image to the screen occupying the same space as the lower objective; mirror movement allows apparatus and slides to alternate; the top stage is useful for projection of drawings and diagrams made while the lecture proceeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify optical layout to allow rapid switching between projected apparatus/views and slides, enable both horizontal and vertical projection, and permit live projection of drawings during lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and safety specifications for a lecture lantern
rubrics_metrics.description: The lantern body is of mahogany lined with fireproof insulator, two doors on one side; superior compound achromatic objectives of specified focal lengths for horizontal and vertical projection; superior prism with silvered face; best quality lime-light burner; complete in case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select materials and construction that prioritize fire safety and optical performance; provide a range of objective focal lengths to suit projection modes and include high-quality prisms and light sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slide apparatus usability: graduated scales to set negative size without focusing on screen
rubrics_metrics.description: Barr & Stroud lantern slide apparatus made in accordance with Prof. Struve's most recent design, with graduated scales which enable an operator without focusing on the screen to quickly obtain a negative of lantern size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include graduated, indexed adjustments on slide holders so operators can set image size and framing quickly and reproducibly, reducing the need for trial-and-error focusing during demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustable condenser requirement: continuous capacity variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustable condensers arranged so that capacity can be varied gradually without interruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For wireless-telegraphy and laboratory purposes, use condensers that allow smooth, uninterrupted variation of capacitance to ensure reliable and precise tuning/operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and standardization of Invar for low thermal expansion applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Invar, the patented alloy of nickel steel, has the smallest known coefficient of expansion; offered as rods, tapes, wire; Invar compensation pendulums and tapes for baseline measurements are divided to the utmost accuracy and standardized at the National Physical Laboratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For precision measurement devices (pendulums, baseline tapes, standard meters) select materials with minimal thermal expansion and obtain items standardized at national laboratories to minimise thermal errors.
